title: Technology and worship
hook: prayer apps, online Qur'an, and the need for real presence

segments.voice: Yesterday: mental health and faith, prayer and therapy side by side. Your line was heal the heart two ways. Today, the thing in your pocket.

The app chimes. 'Asr, it says, and a little compass on the screen swings around to point toward Mecca. The mat goes down, the phone beside it, face up, and the prayer begins. Second rak'ah, forehead on the floor, and the screen lights up: a name, half a message. The prayer carries on. The mind doesn't, quite. What does a phone in the pocket do to a prayer? An old report in al-Bukhari fits.
screen: `THE APP CHIMES FOR 'ASR.` → `THE SCREEN LIGHTS UP MID-PRAYER.` → `AN OLD REPORT FOR A NEW MOMENT.`

segments.voice: The report is told by 'Aisha. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once prayed in a garment with markings on it, a patterned cloth, and during the prayer his eye caught the pattern. When he finished he said, in paraphrase: take this to Abu Jahm and bring me his plain one, because this one just distracted me in my prayer. Right beside it, al-Bukhari keeps a second report, about a curtain with pictures hanging in 'Aisha's house. The Prophet asked for it to be taken down, because its pictures kept coming to him while he prayed. He didn't give up clothes, or curtains. He swapped the one thing that kept pulling at his attention for something plain. The tool stayed. The distraction went. The Qur'an has a word for what was being protected. The chapter called The Believers opens, in Pickthall's translation: "Successful indeed are the believers / Who are humble in their prayers." Muslim teachers call that humility in prayer khushu': stillness, lowered eyes, the whole person turned one way. And in the conversation with the angel Gabriel, the Prophet describes ihsan, doing a thing beautifully, in paraphrase: to worship Allah as though you see Him, and though you don't see Him, He sees you. That is presence. So the question about technology is an old one. An app that tells you when Maghrib comes is a timetable. A screen that shows the Qur'an is a page. Both can serve the prayer. 'Aisha's report asks something simpler and harder: what keeps coming to you while you pray, and can you hand it to Abu Jahm?
screen: `A PATTERNED GARMENT, HANDED BACK.` · `A CURTAIN TAKEN DOWN.` · `THE TOOL STAYS. THE DISTRACTION GOES.` · `KHUSHU': THE WHOLE PERSON TURNED ONE WAY.` · then, large: `AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: Set the phone in another room, or face down out of reach, and notice any pull toward it, an itch to check; don't fight it, just notice it, the way the Prophet noticed the pattern on the cloth. Then let your attention come back to one thing: your breath, the room around you, or, if you pray, al-Fatiha said slowly in your head. When the pull comes again, notice it, and come back again.
Technology and worship. Apps, screens and timetables that can serve a prayer, and the presence that no tool can supply. Today's word.
Your line: real presence. The tool stays; the distraction goes. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-two, done.

chat.says: Is it wrong to use a prayer app, or read the Qur'an off a phone?
options: Not in itself. Tools can serve the prayer; the question is what pulls you away.
Yes. Any phone near the prayer mat makes the prayer itself invalid.
Yes. The Prophet gave up every patterned cloth and curtain he owned.
